paragraphs: I believe it is easier to set up an absolute, despotic government among a people whose conditions are equal than among any other. And I think that once such a government was established among such a people, it would not only oppress men; in time it would strip each of them of several of the highest qualities of humanity. Despotism therefore seems to me especially to be feared in democratic ages. I believe I would have loved freedom in any age, but in the age we live in I am ready to worship it. On the other hand, I am convinced that everyone who tries, in the ages we are entering, to base freedom on aristocratic privilege will fail, and so will everyone who tries to gather and hold authority within a single class. Today no ruler is skillful or strong enough to found a despotism by restoring permanent distinctions of rank among his subjects. No legislator is wise or powerful enough to preserve free institutions unless he makes equality his first principle and his watchword. All of our contemporaries who want to establish or protect the independence and dignity of their fellow men must show themselves friends of equality, and the only worthy way to show it is to be so. The success of their sacred enterprise depends on this. So the question is not how to rebuild aristocratic society, but how to bring liberty out of the democratic state of society in which God has placed us.

These two truths seem to me simple, clear, and rich in consequences, and they lead me naturally to ask what kind of free government can be established among a people whose conditions are equal. The very constitution of democratic nations and their needs have this result: the power of government among them must be more uniform, more centralized, more extensive, more probing, and more effective than in other countries. Society as a whole is naturally stronger and more active, and individuals are more dependent and weak. Society does more and individuals do less, and this cannot be otherwise. So we should not expect private independence ever to reach as far in democratic countries as in aristocratic ones, nor is that to be wished. Among aristocratic nations the many are often sacrificed to the individual, and the prosperity of the greater number to the greatness of a few. The government of a democratic people needs to be active and powerful, and it is desirable that it should be. Our aim should not be to make it weak or sluggish, but only to keep it from abusing its capacity and its strength.

What did most to protect the independence of private persons in aristocratic ages was that the supreme power did not claim to take the government and administration of the community wholly on itself. Those functions were necessarily left in part to the members of the aristocracy. Since the supreme power was always divided, it never pressed with its whole weight, or in the same way, on each individual. Not only did the government not do everything through its own direct agency. Most of the agents who carried out its duties drew their power not from the State but from their birth, and so they were not under its constant control. The government could not make or unmake them in an instant at its pleasure, or bend them into strict uniformity to its slightest whim. This was a further guarantee of private independence. I readily admit that we cannot turn to the same means today, but I find certain democratic expedients that may take their place. Instead of placing in the government alone all the administrative powers taken from corporations and nobles, some of them can be entrusted to secondary public bodies, made up temporarily of private citizens. In this way the liberty of individuals will be more secure, and their equality will not be reduced.

The Americans, who care less about words than the French do, still call their largest administrative districts “counties.” But a provincial assembly performs part of the duties of the count or lord-lieutenant. In an age of equality like ours, it would be unjust and unreasonable to create hereditary officers, but nothing prevents us from substituting elected public officials to a certain extent. Election is a democratic expedient. It secures the independence of the public official from the government as well as, and even better than, hereditary rank can in aristocratic nations. Aristocratic countries are full of wealthy and influential people who can look after themselves and cannot easily or secretly be oppressed. Such people keep a government within general habits of moderation and restraint. I am well aware that democratic countries contain no such people by nature, but something comparable can be created by artificial means. I firmly believe that an aristocracy cannot be founded in the world again. But I think that private citizens, by joining together, can form bodies of great wealth, influence, and strength, matching the individuals of an aristocracy. In this way, many of the greatest political advantages of aristocracy would be gained without its injustice or its dangers. An association formed for political, commercial, or manufacturing purposes, or even for science and literature, is a powerful and well-informed member of the community. It cannot be disposed of at will, or oppressed without protest, and by defending its own rights against the government’s encroachments it saves the common liberties of the country.

In periods of aristocracy, each man is always so closely tied to many of his fellow citizens that he cannot be attacked without their coming to his aid. In ages of equality, each man naturally stands alone. He has no hereditary friends whose cooperation he can demand, and no class whose sympathy he can count on. He is easily got rid of, and he is trampled on with impunity. So today an oppressed member of the community has only one means of defending himself: he can appeal to the whole nation, and if the whole nation is deaf to his complaint, he can appeal to mankind. The only way he can make that appeal is through the press. Thus the liberty of the press is infinitely more valuable among democratic nations than among any others; it is the only cure for the evils that equality may produce. Equality isolates men and weakens them, but the press puts a powerful weapon within every man’s reach, one that the weakest and loneliest of them can use. Equality takes away a man’s support from his connections, but the press lets him call all his countrymen and all his fellow men to his aid. Printing has hastened the progress of equality, and it is also one of the best correctives to it.

I think that people living in aristocracies can, strictly speaking, do without the liberty of the press, but this is not true of those who live in democratic countries. To protect their personal independence, I do not rely on great political assemblies, on parliamentary privilege, or on declarations of the sovereignty of the people. All of these can, to some extent, be reconciled with personal servitude, but that servitude cannot be complete if the press is free. The press is the foremost democratic instrument of freedom.

Something similar can be said of the judicial power. It belongs to the essence of judicial power to attend to private interests and to fasten with a special liking on the small matters brought before it. Another essential quality of the judicial power is that it never volunteers its help to the oppressed, but is always available to the humblest person who asks for it. However weak the complainants may be, their complaint will force itself on the ear of justice and demand redress, for this is inherent in the very constitution of the courts. A power of this kind is therefore especially suited to the needs of freedom at a time when the government’s eye and hand are constantly reaching into the smallest details of human actions, and when private persons are too weak to protect themselves and too isolated to count on the help of others. The strength of the courts has always been the greatest security that can be offered to personal independence, and this is especially true in democratic ages. Private rights and interests are in constant danger unless the judicial power grows more extensive and stronger to keep pace with the growing equality of conditions.

Equality awakens in men several inclinations that are extremely dangerous to freedom, and the legislator should keep his attention constantly fixed on them. I will only remind the reader of the most important. Men living in democratic ages do not readily grasp the usefulness of forms; they feel an instinctive contempt for them, and I have shown elsewhere why. Forms arouse their contempt and often their hatred. Since they generally aim only at easy and immediate satisfactions, they rush toward what they desire, and the slightest delay exasperates them. This same temper, carried into political life, makes them hostile to forms, which constantly slow or halt them in some of their projects. Yet the very objection that men in democracies make to forms is what makes forms so useful to freedom. Their chief merit is to serve as a barrier between the strong and the weak, between ruler and people, to hold back the one and give the other time to look around. Forms become more necessary as the government grows more active and more powerful, while private persons grow more idle and more feeble. So democratic nations naturally need forms more than other nations do, and naturally respect them less. This deserves the most serious attention. Nothing is more pitiful than the arrogant disdain most of our contemporaries show for questions of form, since even the smallest of them have gained in our time an importance they never had before, and many of mankind’s greatest interests depend on them. I think that if the statesmen of aristocratic ages could sometimes scorn forms with impunity, and often rise above them, then the statesmen to whom the government of nations is now entrusted should treat even the least of them with respect, and should not neglect them unless necessity compels. In aristocracies, forms were observed superstitiously; among us they should be kept with a deliberate and informed deference.

Another tendency, which is entirely natural to democratic nations and extremely dangerous, leads them to despise and undervalue the rights of private persons. The attachment men feel to a right, and the respect they show it, is generally proportional to its importance or to how long they have enjoyed it. Among democratic nations, the rights of private persons are usually of little importance, recent in origin, and extremely precarious. The result is that they are often sacrificed without regret and almost always violated without remorse. But it happens that in the same period, and among the same nations, in which men naturally come to despise the rights of private persons, the rights of society at large are naturally extended and consolidated. In other words, men become less attached to private rights at exactly the time when it would be most necessary to keep and defend what little remains of them. It is therefore above all in the democratic ages we live in that the true friends of human liberty and greatness should constantly be on guard, to prevent the power of government from lightly sacrificing the private rights of individuals to the general carrying out of its plans. In such times no citizen is so obscure that it is not very dangerous to let him be oppressed, and no private right is so unimportant that it can be given up with impunity to a government’s whims. The reason is clear. If an individual’s private right is violated at a time when the human mind is fully impressed with the importance and sanctity of such rights, the harm is confined to the individual whose right is infringed. But to violate such a right today is to corrupt the customs of the nation deeply and to endanger the whole community, because the very idea of this kind of right keeps tending, among us, to be weakened and lost.

Certain habits, certain ideas, and certain vices are peculiar to a state of revolution, and a long revolution cannot fail to produce and spread them, whatever its character, its purpose, or the place where it occurs. When a nation has repeatedly changed its rulers, its opinions, and its laws within a short time, the men who make it up eventually acquire a taste for change and grow used to seeing every change brought about by sudden violence. So they naturally come to despise forms that prove ineffective day after day, and they do not bear patiently the rule of regulations they have so often seen broken. The ordinary ideas of fairness and morality no longer suffice to explain and justify all the innovations a revolution gives birth to every day. So the principle of public utility is summoned, the doctrine of political necessity is conjured up, and men grow used to sacrificing private interests without scruple and to trampling on the rights of individuals in order to accomplish any public purpose more quickly.

These habits and ideas, which I will call revolutionary because every revolution produces them, appear in aristocracies just as much as among democratic nations. But in the former they are often less powerful and always shorter-lived, because there they meet habits, ideas, defects, and obstacles that work against them. Consequently they vanish as soon as the revolution is over, and the nation goes back to its former political ways. This is not always so in democratic countries, where it is always to be feared that revolutionary tendencies, becoming gentler and more regular without disappearing entirely from society, will gradually turn into habits of submission to the administrative authority of the government. I know of no countries in which revolutions are more dangerous than democratic ones. Apart from the accidental and passing evils that always go with them, they may always create some evils that are permanent and endless. I believe there is such a thing as justifiable resistance and legitimate rebellion. So I do not assert, as an absolute rule, that men in democratic ages should never make revolutions. But I think they have particular reason to hesitate before embarking on one, and that it is far better to put up with many grievances in their present condition than to turn to so dangerous a remedy.

I will conclude with one general idea, which contains not only all the particular ideas expressed in this chapter but also most of those this book sets out to treat. In the aristocratic ages before our own, there were private persons of great power, and a social authority of extreme weakness. The outline of society itself was hard to make out and was constantly confused with the various powers that ruled the community. The main efforts of the men of those times had to go into strengthening, enlarging, and securing the supreme power, and, on the other side, into confining individual independence within narrower limits and subordinating private interests to the public interest. Other dangers and other cares await the men of our age. Among most modern nations, the government, whatever its origin, its constitution, or its name, has become almost all-powerful, and private persons are sinking more and more into the lowest stage of weakness and dependence. In the older society, everything was different: unity and uniformity were found nowhere. In modern society, everything threatens to become so alike that the distinctive traits of each individual will soon be lost entirely in the general appearance of the world. Our forefathers were always inclined to misuse the idea that private rights ought to be respected. We, for our part, are naturally inclined to exaggerate the idea that the interest of a private individual ought always to give way to the interest of the many. The political world has been transformed, and new remedies must now be sought for new disorders. These seem to me the main objects for legislators in the ages we are now entering: to set wide but clear and settled limits on the action of the government; to give private persons certain rights and secure their undisputed enjoyment of them; to enable the individual to keep whatever independence, strength, and original power he still has; and to raise him up beside society at large and sustain him in that position. It would seem that the rulers of our time want only to use men in order to make things great. I wish they would try a little more to make men great. I wish they would value the work less and the worker more, and never forget that a nation cannot long remain strong when each of its members is weak, and that no form or combination of social order has yet been devised that can make an energetic people out of a community of timid and enfeebled citizens.

I see two opposite ideas among our contemporaries, and both are equally harmful. One group of men can see nothing in the principle of equality except the anarchic tendencies it produces. They dread their own free will; they fear themselves. Other thinkers, fewer in number but better informed, take a different view. Besides the path that runs from the principle of equality to anarchy, they have at last found the road that seems to lead men to inevitable servitude. They shape their souls in advance to this necessary condition, and, despairing of staying free, they already bow in their hearts to the master who will soon appear. The first group give up freedom because they think it dangerous, the second because they think it impossible. Had I held the second conviction, I would not have written this book; I would have limited myself to grieving in secret over the fate of mankind. I have tried to point out the dangers that the principle of equality poses to human independence because I firmly believe these dangers are the most formidable, and the least foreseen, of all those the future holds in store. But I do not think they are insurmountable. Men living in the democratic ages we are entering naturally have a taste for independence. They are naturally impatient of regulation, and they tire even of the permanence of the condition they themselves prefer. They are fond of power, but they tend to despise and hate those who wield it, and by their own mobility and insignificance they easily slip out of its grasp. These inclinations will always show themselves, because they originate in the foundations of society, which will not change. For a long time they will prevent any despotism from being established, and they will supply new weapons to each generation that struggles on behalf of human liberty. Let us then look to the future with that healthy fear which makes men stand watch and guard for freedom, and not with that faint and idle terror which depresses and weakens the heart.
